why: Paula was a Roman noblewoman who gave up her wealth and settled at Bethlehem with her daughter Eustochium, near Jerome. Later Catholic writers use her as the model widow and learned holy woman. The English Life of Lady Montague holds her up to its heroine, and Sor Juana names her as a woman scholar who read Hebrew, Greek and Latin.
reason: The counted passages are sound, but the only writing in her name is a letter Jerome says he composed for her. Mark needs to rule whether that is a document 'issued in her name' under Answer C. If he says yes, this becomes an include.
doubts: (1) Own words rest on Letter XLVI alone; ghost-written by Jerome per the edition headnote. (2) She co-founded the Bethlehem houses; no census movement is named for her, so founder_of is null, but a reviewer may want to confirm. (3) The recusant witness (Smith 1627) is a badly OCR-garbled scan; the quote keeps the garbling ('bewayled bim', '5he'). Nine hits there are all Jerome-on-Paula, mostly repeated citations of the same Epitaph. (4) Colonial count is exactly 5: four in Sor Juana's own prose and devotional texts plus one Villagomez deposition. Namesakes were excluded by the first pass (Francis of Paula, Fray Francisco de Paula). I read refs 215, 1068, 1412 (recusant) and 6677, 7471, 10724, Villagomez 439 (colonial); all name Paula of Bethlehem.

name: Basilides
own_words: none held. The Library has no work of his. What survives is a few passages quoted by opponents, for example Clement of Alexandria quoting the twenty-third book of his Exegetics (Stromata IV.12) and Hippolytus's Refutation Book VII. The census itself says he is 'known only through hostile summaries'.
party_in_own_right: The corpus treats him as the head of a distinct Alexandrian school with its own system, but always through the hostile accounts of others.

why: Basilides taught at Alexandria in the early second century and built a system of his own, separate from Valentinus. Later writers name him as the standard example of a heresy that took its founder's name. We know his teaching almost only from Clement, Hippolytus and other critics.
reason: No writing of his is held and no recorded position of his own; every word of his comes through opponents, which Answer C excludes. The Roman and Montanist counts are the same seven passages from one Hippolytus text.
doubts: (1) Roman Church and Montanism list identical refs (the same seven Refutation Book VII passages), so they are one witness counted twice. Only Alexandria-catechetical is an independent text set, and most of its hits mention his followers, not him. (2) Hippolytus's Basilides and Irenaeus's Basilides differ in what they report, so which man is described is itself disputed. (3) Namesakes were screened out by the first pass: Basilides of Leon, of Pentapolis, and the prefect in the Potamiaena martyrdom. (4) Quoted fragments (Clement, Stromata IV.12, lines 38952-38957) are verbatim quotation by an opponent, which the brief says does not count as his own words. (5) I read refs 41336, 30651 (Alexandria) and 10886, 11231, 11379 (Roman/Montanist). One Alexandria ref (Origen on Matthew 12477) is a bare name-list mention.

why: Novatian held that the church could not take back Christians who had sacrificed under Decius. His supporters made him a rival bishop in 251 and his Katharoi churches lasted for centuries. Ambrose and Jerome still argue against him a century and more later.
reason: The census movement Novatianism is named for him and grew from his consecration, so this is a founder question for Mark. Counts and own works are otherwise sound.
doubts: (1) Founder: Novatianism, id novatianism. (2) Home is ambiguous: his own works are role tradition on both novatianism and roman-church-third-century; I give Novatianism because the census lists him as its voice 0. (3) Ambrosian count is 6 distinct passages (33920/33921 are one sentence); Ambrose speaks to 'Novatian' as the heresiarch and the sect together. (4) Jerome's nine mix Letter XLII (rebuking a Novatian reading of Matthew 12:32) with Lives of Illustrious Men entries (npnf203 lines 40803, 40852, 41087) and Apology 53846, where Novatian is named as an author or a party. (5) Cyprian's letters join Novatian with Novatus, a different man; those were excluded and the Cappadocian count was rejected as outside the shelved works. I read Ambrose 33607, 33920 and Jerome 8404, 8419, npnf203 40803, 40852, 41087, 53846.

home_citation.text: Apollinaris of Laodicea (c. 310-c. 390) and his school (the Greek texts and fragments)

why: Apollinaris argued that the divine Word took the place of a human mind in Christ. Councils condemned the view, and later Byzantine and North African writers still use his name as the type of that error. His followers kept his works alive under other men's names.
reason: The position is named for him (Apollinarian Christianity), so this is a founder question for Mark. His authorship is also partly in doubt because his works circulated under other names.
doubts: (1) Founder: apollinarian-christianity. (2) The Lietzmann attributions are the editor's reconstruction, and the school's works circulated under Athanasius's and Gregory's names (Evagrius says so, evagrius file line 6872); a reviewer should check which fragments are firmly his. (3) Byzantine count is exactly 5 and leans on documents inside other works: Leo's letters 4644 and 4723, Constantinople II acts 23665 and 23748, Evagrius 6872. 4644 is part of a letter by Eutyches inside Leo's collection. (4) Namesakes: Sidonius Apollinaris, Apollinaris of Valence, of Ravenna, of Hierapolis, Apollinarius of Alexandria; the first pass excluded them. The PL67 Dionysius passage with unclear referent was left out. (5) The brief says home is where his own works sit as role tradition; that is the Apollinarian shelf.

reason: A principal with a letter issued in his name; he founded no census movement (he approved Francis's friars but did not found them); and both counted traditions hold at least five separate passages by my own search.

Tridentine: Roman Catechism 14284 and 17445; Barlow Brutum Fulmen 1282, 1502, 16399; Pallavicino 2036, 10423, 11984; Propaganda Fide 40633, 42216, 44042; Missal 1553, 1807, 4103; Sarpi 77955.
